text: Welcome to Python for Data Science — step two of the Data Scientist path. In T-SQL Development you learned to pull data out of databases. Here you learn the tool that lets you clean it, reshape it, and analyze it at scale. This course teaches Python from zero, but only the parts data work actually needs — no web frameworks, no game programming, no object-oriented theory. Before any of that, you need a working setup, and the most valuable habit to build on day one is the virtual environment.

Here's what this lesson covers: installing Python 3 and confirming it works, understanding why every project should get its own virtual environment, creating and activating one, and installing packages while recording exactly what you installed.

Download Python 3 from python dot org and run the installer, ticking the box to add Python to your PATH on Windows. Open a terminal and run python, space, dash dash version — you should see something like Python 3.9.13; any recent Python 3 works fine for this course. You can also ask Python where it lives: importing sys and printing sys dot executable shows the exact interpreter that's running, which matters once you have more than one Python on your machine.

Every package you install has a version, and different projects need different versions. Install everything into one global Python, and an upgrade for one project can silently break another. A virtual environment fixes that: a private folder holding its own interpreter and packages. Create one with python dash m venv dot venv. Activate it with the Scripts activate script on Windows, or source bin activate on Mac and Linux — your prompt shows the environment name once it's active.

With the environment active, pip installs into that environment only. Install numpy, pandas, and matplotlib, then run pip freeze, redirected into a file called requirements dot txt — that file lists every installed package with its exact version. Anyone, including future you, can rebuild the identical environment later with one command: pip install dash r requirements dot txt. Keep the environment folder itself out of version control; commit requirements dot txt instead.

Many data teams use Anaconda or Miniconda instead — distributions that bundle Python with a package manager called conda. The equivalent commands are conda create, naming an environment and a Python version, then conda activate. The habit is identical either way: one environment per project, and a written record of what's inside it. This course uses venv and pip in its examples, and everything you learn transfers directly to conda.

To recap: install Python 3 and confirm it with python dash dash version, create a project environment with python dash m venv dot venv and activate it, then install with pip install and record with pip freeze. Next lesson: Jupyter Notebooks, the interactive workspace where most data work actually happens.
